extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in UK administrative law (law students, legal practitioners, general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: A short Wikipedia article summarising the Court of Appeal decision in BBC v Johns (1964/1965), focusing on the holding about royal prerogative and tax exemption. Meant to provide a concise statement of facts, judgment, and legal significance for general and legal audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on creating new prerogative powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The court disagreed, ruling that it is not possible to create new prerogative powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expresses the legal principle that the executive (or government) cannot, by its own action, expand or invent new royal prerogative powers; such creation or extension is not permissible absent law. The page also records Lord Diplock's dictum: "350 years and a civil war too late for the Queen’s courts to broaden the royal prerogative."

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax exemptions must be granted by legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tax exemptions could only be granted by legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holds that claims to tax immunity or exemption cannot be sustained on the basis of alleged prerogative status alone; statutory authority is required for tax exemptions. This was the basis for rejecting the BBC's claim to be exempt from income tax.

rubrics_metrics.name: No automatic Crown immunity for entities alleging prerogative origin
rubrics_metrics.description: The BBC does not enjoy Crown immunity from taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to facts where BBC argued it was a monopoly established by royal prerogative and therefore exempt from income tax; the court rejected that contention and found no automatic Crown immunity simply from asserted prerogative origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritative dictum as precedent for limits on prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: Lord Diplock's statement (dictum) emphasises the court's view that it is too late for courts to broaden the royal prerogative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although framed as a memorable phrase, the dictum functions as a guiding statement about judicial restraint regarding expansion of prerogative powers and is commonly cited for the principle limiting prerogative development by the courts.
